title: Agent Evaluation
summary: This intermediate module teaches you to design and interpret structured evaluations of agent behavior. After completing it, you can define observable success criteria, examine action traces, compare repeated trials, and report limitations that an outcome-only review could miss.
objectives: Define an agent evaluation task with observable success criteria and failure conditions.
Assess both the final outcome and the sequence of actions that produced it.
Use repeated, comparable trials to identify behavior that may not be consistent.
Report evaluation findings without generalizing beyond the tasks and conditions tested.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previous citation was the local repository path content/modules/reliable-agent-workflows/agent-evaluation.json. It had an unregistered publisher and had never been verified, so it could not serve as a public, resolvable source.

This update replaces that citation with a canonical research-paper URL and official risk-management guidance. The change affects the source record and the explanation of why evaluations should use documented measurements, realistic tasks, and stated limits. The instructional focus on task outcomes, action traces, repeated trials, and bounded conclusions is otherwise unchanged.
sections.callout: Source correction: the unverified local citation was removed and replaced with public HTTPS sources listed at the end of this module.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you understand the basic idea of an agent as a system that pursues a goal through a sequence of observations and actions. It does not assume advanced statistical knowledge or familiarity with any named evaluation product.

Agent evaluation asks whether an agent completes a defined task under stated conditions and whether its behavior remains acceptable while doing so. A useful evaluation therefore examines more than the final answer. It also records relevant actions, intermediate results, failures, and evaluation conditions.

sections.title: Define the evaluation before running it
paragraphs: Begin with a task that has a clear starting state and an observable completion condition. Write the success criteria before examining the agent's result. This reduces the temptation to reinterpret an unexpected result as success after the trial.

Also define failure conditions. These can include an incorrect outcome, an unfinished task, an action outside the permitted scope, or a result that cannot be supported by the recorded evidence. Keep the conditions relevant to the task rather than adding measurements that do not help answer the evaluation question.

Record the conditions needed to interpret the trial, such as the task instructions, available information, permitted actions, and stopping rule. Comparisons are meaningful only when the evaluator knows which conditions were held constant and which were intentionally changed.

sections.title: Inspect outcomes and action traces
paragraphs: Score the final outcome against the criteria defined before the trial. Then inspect the action trace, meaning the recorded sequence of observations, decisions, actions, and intermediate results that led to that outcome.

Outcome and trace evidence answer different questions. The outcome shows whether the task was completed. The trace can reveal unsupported reasoning, unnecessary actions, recovery from an error, or behavior that violated a stated limit even when the final result appeared correct.

A correct outcome does not automatically establish an acceptable process. Likewise, a failed outcome may contain a useful trace showing exactly where the behavior diverged from the expected path. Report both kinds of evidence rather than collapsing them into a single unexplained label.

sections.title: Repeat comparable trials
paragraphs: When behavior can vary between runs, one successful trial does not establish consistent performance. Repeat the task under the same documented conditions and record each result. If you change a condition, label that trial separately so the comparison remains interpretable.

Compare the frequency and type of observed successes and failures without claiming that the results apply to tasks you did not test. A narrow evaluation can provide useful evidence about its defined tasks, but it does not by itself establish general reliability.

When reporting findings, identify the tested tasks, success criteria, relevant conditions, observed limitations, and evidence source. This gives another evaluator enough context to understand what the result supports and what remains untested.

sections.title: A practical evaluation workflow
paragraphs: First, state the task and starting conditions. Second, define observable success and failure criteria. Third, run the task while preserving relevant outcome and trace evidence. Fourth, score the result using the prewritten criteria. Fifth, repeat comparable trials when behavior can vary. Finally, report the findings with their scope and limitations.

After this module, you can perform this workflow instead of relying on an informal impression from one final answer. You can also explain why a result is supported, which behavior caused a failure, and which conclusions remain outside the evidence collected.

questions.prompt: When should success criteria be written for an agent evaluation?
choices: After deciding whether the result looks useful
Only after every repeated trial is complete
Only when the first trial fails
questions.explanation: The module instructs evaluators to define success criteria before examining the result so an unexpected outcome is not reinterpreted as success after the trial.

questions.prompt: Why should an evaluator inspect both the final outcome and the action trace?
choices: The trace replaces the need for success criteria
The outcome and trace provide evidence about different aspects of performance
A correct outcome proves that every action was acceptable
A failed outcome makes the trace irrelevant
questions.explanation: The outcome shows whether the task was completed, while the trace can reveal errors, unnecessary actions, recovery behavior, or violations of stated limits.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate response when agent behavior can vary between runs?
choices: Treat the first successful run as proof of consistent performance
Change several conditions without recording them
Repeat the task under documented, comparable conditions
Discard failed trials and report only successful ones
questions.explanation: The module recommends repeated trials under the same documented conditions when behavior can vary. Changed conditions should be labeled separately.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is supported by a narrow evaluation?
choices: The agent is reliable for every possible task
The observed results describe performance on the tested tasks under the stated conditions
Any untested behavior can be inferred from one successful trial
questions.explanation: The module states that conclusions must remain bounded by the tasks and conditions tested. A narrow evaluation does not establish general reliability.
